tour.title: Varanasi: Life, Death and the Ganges
tour.summary: Dawn bells at Assi, poets and kings along the river stairs, lunch in the old-city lanes, and the evening lamps of Dashashwamedh — one walk through the oldest living city on earth.
tour.overviewText:
Welcome to Varanasi. Or Banaras. Or Kashi, the Luminous — the city of light, which is what the oldest texts call it, and they are not exaggerating. People have lived, prayed and been cremated on this riverbank for something like three thousand years, without a break. You are about to walk through all of it, in about four kilometres.

Here is the shape of the walk. We start at dawn at Assi Ghat, the southern end of the riverfront, where the city wakes up with bells and chanting. Then we walk north along the ghats — the great stone staircases that are Varanasi's front porch, back garden and church all at once. You will meet a poet-saint, a truth-obsessed king, and a version of Shiva who prefers the south of India. You will stand where the creator-god Brahma sacrificed ten horses. Then we turn inland to the golden temple of Kashi Vishwanath and the food lanes of the old city, where breakfast is a competitive sport. We return to the river at Manikarnika, the cremation ghat, which we visit quietly and respectfully from the riverside. And we finish at Scindia Ghat in the north, looking at a temple that is slowly sinking into the Ganges.

And one thing to understand before any of it, because it explains half of what you are about to see. For Hindus, Varanasi is the place to die. The belief is that to die here — to be cremated on these ghats, ashes to this river — is to step off the wheel of rebirth entirely: moksha, liberation, no coming back. So they come. Families travel across India with their dead. Old people check into hospices like Mumukshu Bhavan and Kashi Labh Mukti Bhavan to wait for death in the holy city. The smoke you will see rising over the river is not an accident of the city. It is the point of the city.

Modern Varanasi wears its holiness in public. This is the prime minister's constituency — Narendra Modi has held this seat since 2014 — and the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor, opened in 2021, bulldozed a dense old neighbourhood to give pilgrims a grand walkway to the temple. Supporters call it overdue renewal; critics mourn what was demolished to build it. You will walk the result. And the Ganges itself is both goddess and open sewer: the Namami Gange cleanup has made stretches visibly better, and plenty of stretches are not. Hold the sacred and the polluted in your head at the same time. So does everyone here.

Two house rules before we start. Rule one: the ghats are steps — hundreds of them, steep, uneven, and slippery near the water. This walk is not step-free, and I will not pretend otherwise. Wear shoes with grip, not flip-flops, and budget your knees. Rule two: every price I mention is an educated guess. Indian prices move, temple rules change, and the aarti starts when it starts. Verify at the gate, check the day's timings, and never blame the nice voice in your ear.

And one last thing, and this one matters. Varanasi is not a museum. People bathe, mourn, marry, eat and argue all around you, often at the same time. Walk slowly. Do not photograph bathers or cremations. When I tell you to put the camera away, I mean it. The river rewards the patient and embarrasses the hurried.
tour.difficulty: Moderate. Mostly flat walking along the ghat tops, but with many steep, uneven stone steps up and down between ghats and the old-city lanes. Ghat steps are not step-free and can be slippery near the water.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at dawn, around 5:30 to 6am at Assi, for the morning aarti, soft light and the ghats at their most alive. Time the middle of the walk for the temple and lunch, and be back at the river for the Dashashwamedh evening aarti at about 7pm — either linger along the way or rest midday and return. Winter mornings can be foggy, which is atmospheric but slow.

stops.name: Assi Ghat
stops.narration:
Good morning. You have started at the very beginning — or rather, at the very south. This is Assi Ghat, the southernmost of the great ghats, and the place where Varanasi wakes up.

Look at the river first. That enormous, calm, brown-green sheet of water is the Ganges — Ganga, the goddess as much as the river. She has flowed past this exact spot since before anyone wrote anything down, and every single morning, without fail, this city comes down these steps to meet her. Bathing, chanting, yoga, laundry, gossip. The ghats are where Varanasi does its living, and Assi is the living room.

The name comes from the little Assi river, which once met the Ganges here. It is mostly a drain now, which is sad, but the mythology refused to leave. This is where the poet-saint Tulsidas is said to have lived and coughed his way through old age, and where pilgrims traditionally begin the five-day Panchakroshi pilgrimage around the holy city. Starting here means you are doing it the orthodox way round: south to north, with the current of holiness, so to speak.

Now lift your eyes to the steps. Every dawn there is a ceremony here — Subah-e-Banaras, the morning of Banaras — with Vedic chanting, classical music and a small fire aarti as the sun comes up. It is the gentle sibling of the famous evening show you will see later. Smaller crowds, mist on the water, priests' bells ringing across the steps. If you only do one early morning in India, make it this one.

Take ten minutes. Watch an old man do his sun salutations next to a buffalo being scrubbed next to a sadhu drinking chai. Nobody here thinks any of that is strange. That is the whole thesis of Varanasi in one frame: everything happens at once, and the river absorbs all of it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat, no ticket and no gate. Boatmen will offer sunrise rides from about ₹100 to ₹300 per person for a shared boat; agree the price and duration before stepping in.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The Subah-e-Banaras morning ceremony runs around sunrise, roughly 5:30 to 7am depending on season. Timings shift with the sun, so check locally.
stops.accessibility: Broad steps down to the water with no ramps and no handrails. The upper promenade is level but the steps themselves are steep and uneven.
stops.insiderTip: Come before sunrise and claim a spot on the middle steps. The morning aarti faces east across the water, and the first light hits the priests' lamps before it hits anything else.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north along the top of the ghats, keeping the river on your right, for about five minutes. The next stop is the quieter ghat with the large peepal tree and the small shrines, just past the bend.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Vijendra319, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Tulsi Ghat
stops.narration:
This quieter stretch of steps is Tulsi Ghat, and it belongs to a poet. Specifically, to Goswami Tulsidas — the sixteenth-century saint who did for Hindi what Shakespeare did for English, except with more monkeys.

Tulsidas lived here, on this ghat, in the 1500s. And here he wrote the Ramcharitmanas — the retelling of the Ramayana in everyday Awadhi Hindi that took the story of Prince Rama out of Sanskrit, which only priests read, and gave it to everyone. Farmers sing it. Grandmothers quote it. Whole neighbourhoods stage it every autumn in the Ramlila plays. One man, sitting above this river, wrote the book that half a billion people grew up on. No pressure on your journaling habit.

The house he lived in is supposed to have stood right above these steps, and the small Lolark Kund — a stepped well sacred to the sun god — sits just behind the ghat in the Bhadaini lanes. Childless couples still come to bathe there, which tells you how seriously this city takes its holy plumbing.

Look for the more modern plaque of devotion: the office of the Sankat Mochan Foundation, run for decades by Veer Bhadra Mishra — a temple priest who was also a hydraulic engineering professor, which is the most Varanasi CV imaginable. He spent his life suing and shaming people into cleaning the Ganga, proving that faith and chemistry can share a desk.

This is a working neighbourhood ghat, not a showpiece. Wrestlers practise in the akhara pits nearby, washermen beat clothes on the stones, and nobody will try to sell you anything. Enjoy the breather. The crowds start building from the next stop north.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat, no ticket. The Lolark Kund well behind the ghat is also free to visit.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The ghat is at its best and busiest around sunrise and sunset.
stops.accessibility: Steep stone steps with no ramps. The lanes behind the ghat are narrow and uneven.
stops.insiderTip: Glance at the painted tiles and wall shrines as you pass — the Ramlila scenes painted around these lanes are touched up every autumn before the festival season.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue north along the ghat-top path for about ten to twelve minutes, passing Bhadaini and Janaki ghats. The next stop is the ghat with the tall crematorium building and the big open burning terraces on your right.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Nandanupadhyay, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Harishchandra Ghat
stops.narration:
Slow down, and lower your voice. This is Harishchandra Ghat — the smaller of Varanasi's two burning ghats — and you are standing at the edge of something profound that is not a performance.

The ghat is named for King Harishchandra, the legendary ruler who gave up his kingdom, his wife and very nearly his son rather than tell a lie. Destitute, he ended up working here, at this cremation ground, for the Dom keeper of the pyres — carrying corpses and collecting firewood to feed his family. The gods, satisfied with his honesty, eventually restored everything. Hindus still invoke his name as shorthand for truthfulness the way you might invoke a saint. And this is his office.

What you are seeing is ordinary Hindu life at its most serious. Bodies wrapped in white or red cloth, carried down on bamboo biers by chanting relatives, cremated on wood pyres so the soul can be released and the ashes given to the river. There is also a modern electric crematorium in the building behind the steps — same sacrament, faster paperwork. Nobody here is acting for tourists. This is Tuesday.

So here are the rules, and they are non-negotiable. Do not photograph the pyres, the bodies or the mourners. Do not stare. Do not let any self-appointed guide guilt you into a donation speech — a polite folded-hands namaste and a firm no thank you works. Keep to the upper steps, keep moving gently, and let the families have their grief in peace.

You will see the great cremation ghat, Manikarnika, later. Harishchandra is its quieter sibling, and the etiquette you practise here is the rehearsal. Walk on softly when you are ready.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat, no ticket. Decline paid guiding offers firmly; donations to pandas or Doms are voluntary and never obligatory.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Cremations happen through the day and night.
stops.accessibility: Steep steps with no ramps. Stay on the upper terrace if the lower steps feel unsteady — the view and the lesson are the same.
stops.insiderTip: The tall chimneyed building is the electric crematorium — many local families use it, and its presence is a reminder that this is a working civic facility, not a spectacle.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north along the steps for just two to three minutes. The next stop is the colourful red-and-white striped temple rising directly over the river, almost next door.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Vrinda, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Kedar Ghat and Kedareshwar Temple
stops.narration:
And just like that, the mood lifts. See that handsome temple striped red and white, rising straight out of the steps like a lighthouse? That is Kedareshwar — the temple of Kedar, a form of Shiva — and this is Kedar Ghat, one of the brightest, busiest, most photogenic corners of the whole riverfront.

Here is the theology, and it is gloriously ambitious. Devotees say that bathing here and praying at this shrine earns you the same merit as making the brutal Himalayan pilgrimage to Kedarnath, Shiva's great mountain temple. Same god, same credit, no frostbite. It is the spiritual equivalent of a generously transferable airline ticket, and the priests will happily stamp your boarding pass.

Look at the crowd. Kedar is the headquarters of Varanasi's south Indian and Bengali pilgrims — you will hear Tamil, Telugu and Bengali mixed with the Hindi, and the temple priests serve them all without missing a beat. The ghat's kund, a square stepped tank just behind the temple, hosts festivals where the water turns into a mirror of lamps. This is Hinduism's great talent on display: infinite local franchises, one head office.

The architecture deserves a minute. The striped paint is relatively recent dressing on a much older shrine, and the whole composition — temple, steps, boats, bathers — is the Varanasi postcard that paints itself. Photographers: this is your spot. The light hits the temple face in the morning, and the boats line up in the foreground like they have been art-directed.

Take your photos here freely — bathers at a distance, never close up — because from here on the ghats get grander and busier, and this may be your last quiet frame.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat and temple courtyard, no ticket. Small voluntary offerings at the shrine are customary but optional.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The temple shrine is generally open from early morning to midday and again in the evening; hours shift seasonally.
stops.accessibility: Steep steps with no ramps. The temple platform above the steps is level once you climb up.
stops.insiderTip: Step into the lane just behind the temple for chai — the stalls here serve pilgrims, not tourists, so it is cheap, strong and fast.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue north along the ghats for about ten minutes, passing Narad, Raja and Munshi ghats. Follow the river bend — the next stop is the grand, wide ghat with the rows of umbrellas and the big evening stage, which you cannot miss.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: J Duval, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Dashashwamedh Ghat
stops.narration:
Welcome to the main stage. This is Dashashwamedh — the chief ghat of Varanasi, the widest staircase on the river, and every evening the setting for the most famous religious show in India.

The name is a whole myth in four syllables. Dasha: ten. Ashva: horse. Medha: sacrifice. Legend says the creator-god Brahma himself performed ten horse sacrifices right here to welcome Shiva back to the city. A horse sacrifice was the ancient Indian king's ultimate power move — it announced you ruled everything the horse could walk around. Brahma did ten of them, on this spot, which tells you how important this postcode was even to the gods.

By day, it is gloriously ordinary: flower sellers stringing marigolds, barbers shaving pilgrims' heads for mourning rites, boatmen shouting destinations, sadhus posing for photographs for a fee they will name with total confidence. Walk the full width of it. The side shrines and the raised platforms all have stories, and the priests will tell you three of them for the price of one blessing.

Then comes the evening. Every single night, at about seven, seven young priests perform the Ganga aarti on these steps — a synchronised forty-five-minute worship of the river with giant flaming lamps, conches, bells and chanting, mirrored by lamps floated out onto the water. Hundreds of boats pack the river to watch. It is part liturgy, part theatre, entirely sincere, and completely unmissable. Get here by six to claim steps or a boat, and agree boat prices in advance.

If your legs need a rest, this is the place. Sit on the steps, buy a clay cup of chai, and watch the river do what it has done for three millennia: absolutely everything, all at once.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat, no ticket for the aarti, whether you watch from the steps or the water. Shared boats for the evening aarti typically run about ₹200 to ₹500 per person; fix the price and duration before boarding.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. The evening Ganga aarti begins around 7pm most of the year, shifting slightly with the season — confirm the day's time locally. Morning aarti runs near sunrise.
stops.accessibility: Wide, relatively even steps by ghat standards, but still no ramps and no handrails. The crowds at aarti time are dense; arrive early for a stable spot on the upper steps.
stops.insiderTip: The steps beat the boats. Boats drift, jostle and charge surge prices — a high step near the centre gives you the full synchronised-lamp view for free.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the ghat by the main steps up to the street and walk inland, away from the river, for about eight minutes through the lanes. The next stop is the temple with the golden towers at the end of the new corridor — follow the signs for Shri Kashi Vishwanath Dham.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Sujay25, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Kashi Vishwanath Temple and Corridor
stops.narration:
Look up. That flash of gold above the rooftops is the Kashi Vishwanath Temple — the holiest Shiva shrine in one of the holiest cities on earth — and you are standing in the corridor that changed how pilgrims reach it.

The theology first, because it matters here. This temple houses one of the twelve jyotirlingas — pillars of light where Shiva is said to have appeared in person. For Hindus, Kashi is the city Shiva never leaves, and dying here with Vishwanath's name on your lips is the express route to liberation. That is why the cremation ghats exist. That is why the whole city exists. Everything you have walked past today is downstream of this belief.

The history is turbulent enough to need a timeline. The temple has been demolished and rebuilt repeatedly — most famously in 1669 under Aurangzeb, when the Gyanvapi mosque rose beside it, and again in 1780 when the Maratha queen Ahilyabai Holkar rebuilt the present shrine. The gold on the towers came from Maharaja Ranjit Singh in 1835. Then in 2021, the Kashi Vishwanath Dham corridor opened: a grand, security-lined boulevard connecting the temple directly to the river, sweeping away centuries of tangled lanes in one controversial project.

Practically: entry to the temple is free, but phones, cameras, bags and leather goods are not allowed inside — use the lockers, expect airport-style frisking, and dress modestly. There is a paid Sugam Darshan express darshan, roughly ₹300, though prices and rules shift, so verify at the gate. Non-Hindu visitors are welcome in the corridor complex; the sanctum rules are enforced at the door.

Even if you do not go into the sanctum, walk the corridor to the river end. The sightline from the temple to the Ganga, restored after centuries, is the whole point of the project — the city reconnected to its river in one straight gaze.
stops.entranceFeeNote: General entry to the temple is free. A paid Sugam Darshan express queue, around ₹300, is usually available. Lockers for phones and bags are free or nominal. Rules, prices and ID requirements change often, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Generally open from about 3am to 11pm, with sanctum closures duringarti periods. Security lines are shortest in the early morning and longest on Mondays and festival days.
stops.accessibility: The new corridor is wide, paved and mostly level — the easiest walking on this tour. The temple sanctum itself involves crowds, queuing and steps, and is difficult for anyone with limited mobility.
stops.insiderTip: Do not carry your phone to the gate and hope for the best — leave it at your hotel or use the lockers first. The frisking queues move slowly and rejoining them costs you an hour.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk back out to the lanes west of the temple and turn into the narrow bazaar lane heading towards Godowlia. The next stop is the food strip a few minutes' walk away — follow the smell of frying ghee.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gannu03, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Vishwanath Gali Food Lanes
stops.narration:
Stop walking. Start eating. This is Vishwanath Gali and its neighbouring lanes — the old city's stomach — and lunch here is not a meal, it is a contact sport.

The headline act is the Banarasi breakfast, served well into the afternoon by stalls that have not changed their menu in generations. Kachori-sabzi: puffy deep-fried bread, stuffed with spiced dal, drowned in potato curry, with jalebi — orange, syrupy, geometrically perfect spirals — on the side. It costs less than a bus ticket and contains roughly your weekly allowance of ghee. Eat it standing up, off a leaf plate, while the fry cook judges your spice tolerance. This is the correct procedure.

Then the lassi. Varanasi's signature is the thick, creamy kulhad lassi — set in a clay cup, crowned with malai, sometimes flavoured with rose or mango. The famous Blue Lassi Shop, tucked into these lanes since early last century, serves dozens of flavours through a hatch the size of a mailbox, and the walls are papered with foreign banknotes and approval. In winter, look for malaiyyo — saffron-flavoured milk foam served in tiny cups at dawn, which evaporates if you look at it wrong.

A word on safety, because your stomach is doing diplomacy. Eat where the turnover is high and the frying is fresh — the busiest stall is almost always the safest bet. Drink bottled water, skip the raw salads, and let the cooked, the fried and the boiled be your three food groups.

Order one of everything, find a step to sit on, and watch the lane flow past: porters, priests, schoolkids, cows with right of way. The old city runs on ghee and gossip, and for the next half hour, so do you.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Street food is pay-as-you-go: kachori-sabzi around ₹30 to ₹60 a plate, lassi ₹40 to ₹120 depending on flavour. Prices vary by stall, so treat these as a guide.
stops.openingHours: Stalls serve from early morning to late evening. Breakfast items run out by late morning; lassi shops pour all day.
stops.accessibility: Narrow, crowded, uneven lanes with no seating in most stalls. Expect to stand or perch on steps; the ground can be greasy near fry stalls.
stops.insiderTip: Ask for the kulhad — the clay cup — for your lassi, and eat the malai topping with a spoon first. The malaiyyo, if it is winter, sells out by mid-morning, so go early.
stops.nextStopDirections: Head back east towards the river through the lanes, about five minutes downhill. The next stop is the riverside terrace above the cremation ghat — follow the signs for Manikarnika and stay on the upper path.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Adam Jones, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Manikarnika Ghat Viewpoint
stops.narration:
This is the stop that needs the quietest voice. Below you is Manikarnika Ghat — the great cremation ground of Kashi, burning without pause for centuries — and you are here to witness respectfully, from the riverside, and then to move on.

The mythology is that Shiva's earring — mani, jewel; karnika, ear — fell here while he danced with his wife Parvati, marking the spot as eternally sacred. The sacred fire at the ghat, the story goes, has burned ever since, lit by Shiva himself. Whether or not you hold the theology, hold the arithmetic: scores of cremations a day, every day, wood smoke, chanting, and the Dom community who have tended these fires for generations. For Hindus, to be cremated here is to step off the wheel of rebirth. This is not morbid to the people below you. It is the point of the city.

So this is a viewpoint, not a visit. Stay on the upper riverside path. Do not descend among the pyres, do not photograph the cremations or the mourners — photography here is strongly discouraged, and using a camera near the burning platforms will rightly draw anger. Decline the guides who promise a rooftop view for a fee with a polite namaste. Keep your voice down, keep your distance, and keep your time here brief.

What you can do is think. Varanasi puts death in the middle of life — next to the laundry, the cricket, the chai stalls — and refuses to look away. Most of us spend our lives pretending otherwise. Standing here, watching the smoke rise over the river that has carried ashes for three thousand years, you get to borrow, for five minutes, a civilisation that made peace with the one fact the rest of us keep dodging.

When you are ready, walk on north. The city gives you somewhere gentle to put all of this: the quiet northern ghats, a few minutes away.
stops.entranceFeeNote: No ticket. Do not pay for rooftop or guided views of the burning platforms; observe briefly and freely from the public riverside path.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Cremations continue through the day and night; visit in daylight for the clearest, most respectful viewing from the path.
stops.accessibility: The viewpoint is on the upper riverside path with steps nearby and no ramps. Do not attempt the lower burning terraces, which are uneven, crowded and inappropriate for visitors to enter.
stops.insiderTip: Put the camera away entirely at this stop — not just the shutter, the visible camera. The kindest thing you can do here is be obviously, deliberately not photographing.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue north along the riverside path for about three minutes, past Lalita Ghat. The next stop is the ghat with the half-sunken temple leaning in the shallows, just ahead.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gannu03, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Scindia Ghat
stops.narration:
End of the walk — and the river saved you its strangest sight. Look at the waterline: a whole Shiva temple, leaning sideways, half-drowned, with its sanctum below the surface. That is the leaning temple of Scindia Ghat, and it is sinking very, very slowly in front of you.

The story goes like this. The Scindias — the Maratha rulers of Gwalior — built this grand ghat in the 1830s, temple included. But the foundations were too heavy for the riverbank, or the river shifted, or the gods objected to the architecture — pick the explanation that suits your worldview. Part of the ghat collapsed, the temple tilted, and rather than demolish it, everyone shrugged in the most Hindu possible way and carried on worshipping it. The sanctum floods every monsoon. The priests time their rituals around the water level. Faith, it turns out, is waterproof.

This northern stretch is the quiet end of the riverfront. The crowds thin out, the touting stops, the palaces of old princely states — Scindia, Man Singh, the Nepali temple with its wood-carved erotic panels just behind — line the bank like retired actors. Turn around and look south: on a clear evening you can see the whole curve of the ghats, all the way back to where you started at dawn, with the lamps coming on one by one.

So here is your ending. Sit on the steps. The city you have walked through today — poet, king, goddess, cremation fire, breakfast fry cook — is all still going on behind you. Varanasi does not do finales. It just keeps burning, bathing and frying, whether you are watching or not.

You did watch, though. And now the river has seen you too. That, in this city, counts as a relationship. Namaste — and mind the steps on the way up.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open ghat, no ticket. The Nepali temple behind the ghat is free to view from outside.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Late afternoon and sunset give the best light on the sunken temple and the southward view.
stops.accessibility: Steep, uneven steps with no ramps. The sunken temple area itself is partly collapsed — admire it from the stable upper steps.
stops.insiderTip: Look south from the top steps at dusk: the full crescent of lighted ghats is the best panoramic photograph of the walk, and nobody crowds this end.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Climb to the lane behind the ghat and follow it south back towards Godowlia for rickshaws and taxis, or stroll the ghat-top path back towards Dashashwamedh for the evening aarti boats.
